name: Renault
headline: The cash pile and the finance arm cover the market value: the car business comes almost free
one_liner: Renault trades at about €7.7bn while its car business holds €6.6bn of net cash and its captive bank earns roughly €1.5bn of operating profit a year. The market prices the 2026 margin trough as permanent; we think the reset is done and a product cycle is starting.
thesis: The balance sheet is the floor

Automotive net cash of €6.6bn at June 2026 equals about 86% of the market value. Mobilize Financial Services (the former RCI Banque) adds about €1.5bn of annual operating margin and pays dividends to the car business.
The reset is done

Guidance fell from at least 7% margin (early 2025) to about 5.5% for 2026. That guide was confirmed in February, July and October 2026, and the futuREady plan sets a 5-7% through-cycle band. Expectations are now low and credible.
A product cycle is starting

futuREady plans 36 launches by 2030 on a two-year development cycle. Clio VI, Boreal, Twingo E-Tech and Duster are already on sale, and Q3 2026 revenue beat consensus (+1.4% at constant FX versus −0.3% expected).
variant: Chinese competition will crush margins.
Volumes are under pressure, but pricing and mix held. The plan cuts variable cost by about €400 per car a year and development time to two years.
The cash is trapped and will be burnt.
The car business generated €1.5bn of free cash flow in 2025, S&P upgraded Renault to investment grade (BBB−) in December 2025, and the €2.20 dividend was paid from that cash.
Management keeps cutting guidance.
The new CEO reset targets once, in July 2025. The 2026 guide has since been confirmed three times.
Nissan is a black hole.
The stake was written down by €9.3bn in 2025. Our valuation gives it no value, so any monetisation is upside.
business: Renault, Dacia and Alpine brands; a volume player in European B and C segments, with Dacia as the low-cost brand. 52% of European sales were electrified in H1 2026.
Captive car finance and leasing. Contributed €753m of operating margin in H1 2026 and pays dividends up to the car business (€250m in H1 2026, about €500m a year targeted).
About 35% after the 2023-2025 Alliance restructuring, according to press reports. Carried at fair value through equity since June 2025.
No US sales, so US tariffs are a second-order risk. Growth markets are India, Turkey, Morocco and Brazil (Geely partnership in Brazil since September 2026).
macro: Group volumes in Q3 2026. European demand is flat and Chinese brands are gaining share in the low-cost segment where Dacia plays.
The 2026 Middle East conflict lifted raw-material, energy and logistics costs; management expects H2 margin only slightly above H1.
Share of electric cars in Q3 2026 passenger-car sales. EU CO2 rules force the mix shift and compress pricing.
Investment-grade rating (S&P, Dec 2025) lowers funding cost for Mobilize, whose margin depends on rates and used-car prices.

Consensus implies about €6.6 of 2026 EPS (price / 4.3x); we use €6.0 in the base case to stay below the street. The sum of the parts is a sanity check, not the target.

note.intro: Renault is the clearest example in our portfolio of a stock that is cheap because the market does not trust the balance sheet to stay in the hands of shareholders. Our systematic score ranked it first of 102 Consumer Discretionary stocks in December 2025, and the stock has been in the top quintile of its sector at every rebalance since 2021. This note explains how the company makes money, why the market is sceptical, and what has to happen for the discount to close.
business_long: Renault Group sells about 2.3 million vehicles a year (2.337m in 2025) under three brands. Renault is the core volume brand, Dacia is the low-cost brand built around simple platforms and low equipment levels, and Alpine is a small sports-car brand. Most sales are in Europe; Renault has no US business.

The group has two reporting segments since 2026. Automotive makes and sells cars. Mobilize Financial Services (MFS, the former RCI Banque) lends to customers and dealers to finance those cars. MFS is a bank: it takes deposits, funds itself in the bond market and earns a spread. This is why enterprise-value multiples on Renault mislead: you cannot add a bank's debt to a carmaker's equity value and call it an enterprise value.

The third asset is a stake of roughly 35% in Nissan, according to press reports. After the 2023-2025 Alliance restructuring, the stake is held at fair value through equity. Renault took a €9.3bn non-cash accounting loss on it in 2025, which is why reported net income was about −€10.9bn even though the business made an operating margin of 6.3%.
macro_long: European car demand is flat. The pressure comes from Chinese manufacturers such as BYD and Geely, which sell electric cars at prices European brands struggle to match. Dacia is the most exposed because it competes on price: its volumes fell 12.8% in Q3 2026 while the group fell 6.0%.

Costs moved against carmakers in 2026. The Middle East conflict lifted raw materials, energy and freight, and Renault guided to a second half only slightly better than the first. The EU's CO2 rules push the mix toward electric cars, which are less profitable today; Renault's electric share reached 25.8% of passenger cars in Q3 2026.

Rates matter through MFS. Its margin depends on the spread between lending rates and its funding cost, and on used-car prices for leased vehicles. The S&P upgrade to BBB− in December 2025 lowers that funding cost.

note.model_long: At the 31 December 2025 rebalance our lag rule (fiscal year end + 6 months) meant the score used FY2024 accounts. Renault scored above +3 standard deviations on EV/EBIT, book-to-price, FCF yield and sales-to-EV versus its sector. The EV/EBIT of 1.8x is not a real number: the enterprise value nets the automotive cash but ignores the bank's structure. Read the score as a flag, then rebuild the value by parts.
note.bear_long: The bear case is a value trap: margins trend down (7.6% in 2024, 6.3% in 2025, ~5.5% in 2026), the low-cost niche is under attack from China, and the net cash is spent on product launches instead of returned. The medium-term band starts at 5%, so a bad year would sit inside management's own range.
glossary: Operating margin
Renault's main profit measure: operating profit before restructuring and one-offs, divided by revenue.
Automotive free cash flow
Cash generated by the car business after capex and R&D, including the dividend received from MFS.
Captive finance arm
A bank owned by a manufacturer to finance its customers and dealers (here Mobilize Financial Services).
Sum of the parts
Valuing each business separately and adding them, instead of applying one multiple to the whole group.
interview: Why is Renault's EV/EBIT of 1.8x misleading?
Because the group consolidates a bank. Its debt is the bank's funding, not leverage of the car business, so a single EV is meaningless. We value net cash, MFS and the car business separately.
What is the single number that would make you sell?
A 2026 operating margin below 5%, the bottom of management's own band. It would mean the reset was not enough.
Why not value the Nissan stake?
Its value is volatile and its monetisation has no timetable. Giving it zero keeps the thesis independent of Nissan.
How does a value screen end up holding a carmaker for five years?

Carmakers trade on low multiples through the cycle. Renault was in the top quintile of its sector at every date, so the real question is whether the discount closes, which needs cash returned to shareholders.

name: BNP Paribas
headline: A 13% return on tangible equity priced at 0.9x tangible book: the French discount has gone too far
one_liner: BNP earned a 13.2% return on tangible equity over the first nine months of 2026, ahead of its own 12% target, yet trades below tangible book because the market treats it as a proxy for French sovereign risk. With CET1 at 12.9% and a €1.3bn buyback starting, we see value in the gap.
thesis: Returns are ahead of target
9M 2026 RoTE of 13.2% and a 59.0% cost/income ratio beat the 2026 targets (~12% and ~60%). In February 2026 the bank raised its 2028 targets to RoTE above 13% and cost/income below 56%.
The price is a sovereign discount, not a bank discount

Shares fell about 20% in the three months to late October 2026, to a 28-week low of €85.35, with no company-specific cause found, while French 10-year yields reached ~4.9% and the OAT-Bund spread ~155 bp. French government bonds held total about €19bn, €16bn of them at amortised cost.
Capital comes back to shareholders
2026 payout of 60% (at least 50% dividend, 10% buyback), a €1.3bn buyback from November 2026, and from 2027 the distribution of CET1 above 13%. A new 2030 plan is due on 2 February 2027.
variant: BNP is a leveraged bet on France.
Three of its four retail home markets are outside France, CIB is the leading EMEA investment bank, and IPS adds fee income. Earnings are more diversified than the share price implies.
Trading revenue is at a peak.
Global Markets is strong (+21.9% in Q3), but the RoTE target was beaten even after €408m of restructuring costs.
The Sudan litigation is an open-ended liability.
It is real and unprovisioned; we treat it as a tail risk that the appeal (2027) will clarify, and keep the position sized accordingly.
business: Retail networks in France, Belgium, Italy and Luxembourg, Europe-Mediterranean, plus Personal Finance, Arval (car leasing, Athlon acquired July 2026) and Nickel.
Global Banking, Global Markets and Securities Services; the bank describes itself as the leading EMEA investment bank.
Insurance, Wealth Management and Asset Management, including AXA IM, consolidated since July 2025.
CET1 12.9% at September 2026, against a 10.45% requirement; guided above 13% at end-2026.
macro: Political and budget uncertainty pushed French yields up in 2026; French banks trade as a proxy for the sovereign.
A wider spread raises funding costs and the discount investors apply to French financials.
Brent around $115 a barrel with the Middle East conflict: a risk to credit quality and to rate expectations.
Q3 2026, at the top of the <40 bp guide. Arval used-car prices are the visible pressure point.

note.intro: BNP Paribas entered the portfolio at the December 2025 rebalance. Banks are scored only on book-to-price and earnings-to-price in our process, because enterprise value and free cash flow do not make sense for a bank. BNP ranked 5th of 203 financials. This note explains how a universal bank earns money, why its share price moves with French bonds, and how to value it from its tangible book.
business_long: BNP Paribas is the largest bank in the euro area. It has three divisions. Commercial, Personal Banking & Services (CPBS) collects deposits and lends to households and companies in four home markets (France, Belgium, Italy and Luxembourg) and runs specialised businesses such as consumer credit and Arval, a car-leasing company.

Corporate & Institutional Banking (CIB) advises and finances large companies, trades bonds, currencies and equities for clients (Global Markets), and holds assets for institutions (Securities Services). It is about 38% of revenue and the most volatile part of earnings.

Investment & Protection Services (IPS) sells insurance, manages wealth and runs asset management, now including AXA IM. These are fee businesses that need little capital, which is why management keeps adding to them.
macro_long: French government bonds sold off in 2026 on political and budget uncertainty. The 10-year yield reached about 4.9% and the spread over German Bunds about 155 bp. Investors sell French banks when the sovereign weakens, because banks hold government bonds, fund themselves at a spread to the sovereign, and depend on the domestic economy.

For BNP the direct exposure is limited: about €19bn of French government bonds, €16bn of them at amortised cost so price moves do not hit capital. The indirect effect is through funding costs and the risk premium investors demand.

The Middle East conflict pushed Brent to about $115 a barrel. That raises inflation risk and could slow the ECB's path, which helps net interest income but hurts credit quality. BNP's cost of risk was 39 bp in Q3 2026, at the top of its guidance.
history: Manhattan jury finds BNP liable in the Sudan case (~$20.75m to three plaintiffs; class ~23,000)
Shares fall ~20% to €85.35 as French yields rise
Q3 results: net income €3.5bn (+13.5%); €1.3bn buyback announced
note.model_long: At the 31 December 2025 rebalance BNP traded at 0.78x book and 7.7x earnings on FY2024 accounts, against a peer median of 1.2x and 11.6x. Its book-to-price z-score was +2.1 and earnings-to-price +2.0 within Financials. The minimum-variance portfolio gave it only the 0.5% floor; the mean-variance portfolio gave it the 4% cap.
note.bear_long: The bear case: France is in a slow sovereign squeeze, BNP's earnings include one-offs (an €858m gain on Ageas, a €372m Allfunds revaluation) and peak trading, and the Sudan verdict could become a class-wide liability. In that world a bank at 0.9x tangible book is fairly priced, not cheap.
glossary: RoTE
Return on tangible equity: net income divided by equity excluding goodwill and intangibles.
CET1 ratio
Core equity capital divided by risk-weighted assets; the regulator's main solvency measure.
Cost of risk
Loan-loss provisions as a share of outstanding loans, in basis points.
P/TBV
Price divided by tangible book value per share; the standard bank valuation multiple.
interview: Why do you value BNP on price to tangible book and not P/E?
Because a bank's earning power is its equity times its return. Justified P/TBV = (RoTE − g) / (CoE − g) links the two: a 12% RoTE with an 11.5% cost of equity justifies about 1.05x.
What drives the discount?
French sovereign risk. The share price fell 20% in a quarter without bad company news, while French yields rose.
What would make you wrong?
RoTE falling below 12%, CET1 below 12.5%, or a material Sudan provision.
Why did your model give BNP 4% in mean-variance and 0.5% in minimum variance?
Mean-variance rewards the high expected return from the score; minimum variance penalises the bank's high correlation with the rest of the European book.

name: Carrefour
headline: A grocer priced at a double-digit free-cash-flow yield, with real estate worth more than the equity
one_liner: Carrefour fell to €13 after cutting its 2026 guidance on French riots. At that price the market cap (€9.3bn) is below the appraised value of its property (€14.2bn), and even a reduced cash flow gives a double-digit yield. We buy the cash flow and the assets, not a margin recovery story.
thesis: Cash flow at a discount
Net free cash flow was €1.3bn in 2025 (€1.6bn excluding Italy). Even the 'slight decline' now guided for 2026 leaves a free-cash-flow yield above 10% on a €9.3bn market cap.
Assets cover the enterprise value

The property portfolio in France, Spain and Brazil was independently valued at €14.2bn at end-2025, above the market cap plus year-end net debt (about €13.2bn). Sale-and-leasebacks of 35 stores in October 2026 crystallise part of it.
A simpler group

Italy and Romania are sold, Brazil is fully owned, and the three core countries make about 85% of sales and 99% of recurring operating income. Belgium, Poland and Argentina are under review for disposal.
variant: The French market is structurally broken.
France is a low-margin, price-war market, but Carrefour is No. 2 and the plan already prices €1bn a year of savings, half of them delivered by mid-2026.
The riots are a lasting hit.
Management estimates €80-200m of recurring operating income at risk in 2026. That is a one-year shock on a €2.2bn profit base, not a change in earning power.
The dividend will be cut.
This is the real risk: a 50-60% payout on flat EPS implies €0.80-0.96 against €0.97 paid. We assume a cut in the base case.
business: About half of sales: hypermarkets, supermarkets, convenience and e-commerce, moving toward franchise and location-gérance. ROI margin 1.5% in H1 2026.
Atacadão cash & carry and retail; highest margin (4.0% in H1 2026) but exposed to rates near 15% and the real.
Steady growth and a 3.3% margin in H1 2026.
Belgium, Poland and Argentina: loss-making in H1 2026 (−€34m) and under strategic review.

note.intro: Carrefour ranked first of 76 Consumer Staples stocks on our December 2025 score and has been held since June 2022. It is a classic 'cheap for a reason' retailer: thin margins, a price war at home and emerging-market currency risk. This note explains how a grocer makes money, why the October 2026 guidance cut matters less than the share price suggests, and why the dividend is the real test.
business_long: Carrefour sells food and everyday goods through hypermarkets, supermarkets, convenience stores, cash & carry and online. Grocery is a volume business: Carrefour makes about 2.6 cents of operating profit per euro of sales, so small changes in prices or costs move profit a lot.

The 2030 plan (February 2026) focuses the group on three countries where it is No. 1 or No. 2: France, Spain and Brazil. Italy and Romania have been sold; Belgium, Poland and Argentina may follow. In France the group is moving stores to franchise and location-gérance, which lowers its own costs and capital needs.
The group also owns a large property portfolio, valued by independent experts at €14.2bn at end-2025. Carrefour has started selling stores and leasing them back, which turns that value into cash.
macro_long: France is one of the most competitive grocery markets in Europe. Leclerc, Carrefour, Intermarché and Lidl fight on price, and annual negotiations with suppliers cap how much inflation retailers can pass on. Carrefour's plan answers with 200 private-label products sold at cost to loyalty members, which defends traffic but limits margins.

In October 2026 riots, looting and curfews hit French retail: about 50 Carrefour stores were directly damaged and many more closed as a precaution. The company estimates €80-200m of 2026 operating income at risk and cut its guidance on 20 October; the stock fell 12% intraday the next day.
Brazil is the profit engine but brings macro risk: the policy rate near 15% hurt cash & carry volumes in 2025, and the real and the Argentine peso cost €102m of operating income in translation.

Sale-and-leaseback of 35 stores; €500m bond; RCF extended

note.model_long: At the December 2025 rebalance Carrefour scored +4.7 on sales-to-EV and +3.5 on FCF yield within Consumer Staples, using FY2024 accounts. P/FCF was 5.5x against 17.3x for its peers. Part of that is structural: grocers always look cheap on sales because margins are thin, so the FCF signal carries more information than EV/Sales here.
note.bear_long: The bear case is that Carrefour is a value trap: French margins are permanently lower, the 2030 plan slipped in its first year, and a dividend cut removes the main support of the share price. Low multiples in grocery can simply reflect low returns on capital.
glossary: Recurring operating income (ROI)
Carrefour's operating profit before non-recurring items.
LFL (like-for-like)
Sales growth in stores open in both periods, excluding fuel and calendar effects.
Net free cash flow
Cash generated after capex, lease payments and interest, before dividends and M&A.
Sale-and-leaseback
Selling a store to an investor and renting it back, to release the capital tied up in property.
interview: Why is Carrefour cheap on EV/Sales, and does it matter?
Grocers earn 2-3% margins, so EV/Sales is always low. We focus on the FCF yield, which captures what the business actually returns.
The company just cut guidance. Why buy now?
The cut is a €80-200m one-year hit on a €2.2bn profit base. At €13 the cash-flow yield is above 10% and property covers the enterprise value.
What is the main risk to the thesis?
A dividend cut under the new payout policy. We assume it in the base case and still find value.
How long has it been in the portfolio, and how did it do?
Since June 2022, at 8 of 10 rebalances. In H1 2026 it returned about +20% against +11% for the benchmark.

name: HP Inc
headline: A cash machine priced for decline: about 10x earnings and a 10% free-cash-flow yield
one_liner: HP generates about $3bn of free cash flow a year and returns most of it. At $32 the stock trades at about 10x fiscal 2026 earnings and a 10.6% FCF yield, as if printing were about to collapse. We think memory-cost pressure peaks now and the cost programme supports margins into fiscal 2027.
thesis: Cash yield is the valuation

FY2026 FCF guidance was raised to $3.0-3.2bn in August 2026: about 10.6% of the market cap at the midpoint. HP returned $1.9bn (66% of FCF) to shareholders in FY2025 and raised the dividend to $0.30 a quarter.
The margin squeeze is temporary
Management expects DRAM and NAND costs to peak in Q4 FY2026 (Aug-Oct) and Personal Systems margins (4.6% in Q3) to recover sequentially in FY2027. The $1bn gross savings programme runs to FY2028.
Printing still funds the story

note.intro: HP has been in the portfolio at all ten rebalances since June 2021: it is a permanent resident of the cheap end of the technology sector. In December 2025 it ranked 2nd of 128 IT stocks. This note explains the two halves of the business, why the market prices them for decline, and why the free-cash-flow yield is the right way to value it.
business_long: HP Inc is the PC and printer half of the old Hewlett-Packard, split in 2015. Personal Systems sells notebooks, desktops and workstations to companies and consumers. It is large ($38.5bn) but earns thin margins (about 5%), because PCs are assembled from components bought from others, mostly processors and memory.

Printing sells printers and, more importantly, the ink and toner they consume. Supplies are a recurring revenue stream with high margins (the segment earns 18-19%). Page volumes are falling as offices print less, so the segment shrinks about 2% a year.

HP returns most of its cash: about two thirds of free cash flow through dividends and buybacks. Years of buybacks have pushed book equity below zero, which is why P/B is meaningless and why our model scored HP on the other three ratios.
macro_long: Microsoft ended Windows 10 support in October 2025, which forced companies to replace old PCs. Personal Systems revenue rose 8%, 11% and then 18% in successive quarters, partly from higher prices.
The headwind is memory. DRAM and NAND prices rose sharply in 2026, and PC makers pay more for every machine. HP expects the peak in Q4 FY2026 (August to October).

Tariffs were the 2025 shock: HP moved production out of China. In February 2026 the Supreme Court ruled that IEEPA does not authorise tariffs, and HP is receiving refunds, which flatter FY2026 EPS by $0.19 one-off.

glossary: Free-cash-flow yield
Free cash flow divided by market cap; the cash return an owner would earn at today's price.

Supplies

Liabilities exceed assets on the balance sheet, here because buybacks exceeded retained earnings.
interview: Why value HP on FCF yield rather than P/E?
Because the equity story is cash returned to owners, and FCF is less distorted by restructuring charges and tariff refunds.
Isn't printing a melting ice cube?

Book-to-price was negative and counted against HP (z −1.2), but the other three ratios dominated the composite.

note.intro: Nippon Steel entered the portfolio in June 2025, the month it closed the U.S. Steel acquisition, and ranked first of 62 Materials stocks in December 2025. It is a turnaround inside a cyclical industry, so the value signal is only a starting point. This note explains the three engines of the group, the policy context in the US and China, and how to think about book value when returns are depressed.
business_long: Nippon Steel makes flat and long steel products for cars, construction, shipbuilding and energy. In Japan it runs integrated blast-furnace works. Domestic demand is shrinking, so the company has closed capacity (Kashima upstream) and moved customers to contract prices that pass through input costs.

Overseas is the growth engine. U.S. Steel, bought for about $14.9bn in June 2025, makes it a large US producer. The US government holds a golden share that lets it veto plant closures and capacity cuts. AM/NS India, a joint venture with ArcelorMittal, is expanding from about 9 to 15 Mt a year.

Japanese companies report several profit lines. 'Underlying business profit' strips out inventory valuation effects and is the best measure of operating earning power. FY2025 profit to owners was only ¥17bn because of ¥271bn of impairments and losses on exiting AM/NS Calvert and Usiminas.
macro_long: Global steel is oversupplied. China exported a record of about 119 Mt in 2025, which depresses prices across Asia. That is the main reason the domestic business forecast was cut by ¥90bn in August 2026.
The US is protected. Section 232 tariffs keep imported steel out, so U.S. Steel sells at higher prices. The thesis relies on that protection lasting.

Currency and energy cut both ways. A yen at ¥160 per dollar lifts overseas profits in yen and creates inventory valuation gains (about ¥80bn), while the 2026 Middle East conflict raised raw-material, fuel and logistics costs by about ¥60bn.

Golden share
A special share held by a government that gives veto rights over key decisions.

interview: Why is P/B the right metric for a steelmaker?
Earnings swing with the cycle, book value is more stable. The question is the ROE the book can earn: 10% justifies about 1x.

That U.S. Steel's turnaround depends on tariffs. If protection weakens, the overseas story breaks.

About ¥600bn converting at ~¥733 means roughly 820m new shares. They convert only if the stock rises ~11%, so dilution comes with success.

Whether H1 underlying profit reaches ¥250bn and the H2 run-rate target of ≥ ¥900bn holds.

name: Centene
headline: Cheap for the wrong reason: the screen read stale earnings, and the recovery came from elsewhere
one_liner: In December 2025 Centene was the cheapest health-care stock in our universe, on FY2024 earnings that no longer existed. 2025 adjusted EPS collapsed to $2.08 before a 2026 repricing rebound to a guided floor above $5.20. The stock has recovered; at $67.60 it is fairly priced, and the lesson is about process.
thesis: Why the model bought it

With a six-month accounting lag, the December 2025 score used FY2024 accounts: pre-collapse EBIT and book equity before a $6.7bn goodwill impairment. EV/EBIT, P/B and E/P all screened at the top of the sector.
What actually happened

In July 2025 Centene withdrew guidance on Marketplace risk adjustment and Medicaid cost trends. 2025 adjusted EPS came in at $2.08. Repricing then worked: the 2026 floor was raised four times, from $3.00 to $5.20.
Where it stands now

At $67.60 the stock trades at 13x a 2026 figure that includes about $0.50 of non-recurring items. Membership is shrinking (−8% y/y) and Medicaid still runs at a 93.6% benefits ratio. Upside and downside look balanced.

The 2026 rebound came from repricing and policy, not from the cheapness the model measured. The signal had no defence against a fast fundamental break.
Managed care is a stable compounder.
Margins are thin: each 10 bp of benefits ratio on ~$175bn of premiums is about $175m of pre-tax profit.
Guidance raises mean upside.
The floor format ('greater than $5.20') and ~$0.50 of non-recurring items flatter 2026; FY2027 guidance in February is the real test.

note.intro: Centene is in this pitch set as a case study. It shows the main weakness of a value screen that uses lagged accounts: when earnings break fast, trailing multiples fall faster than the price only because the earnings are stale. Centene ranked first of 108 health-care stocks in December 2025 and was held at all ten rebalances. This note explains how a managed-care insurer makes money, what went wrong in 2025 and what the episode teaches.
business_long: Centene is a health insurer paid by governments and individuals to cover medical costs. It receives a premium per member and pays the doctors, hospitals and pharmacies. The key number is the health benefits ratio (HBR): medical costs divided by premiums. At 90% the insurer keeps 10 cents per dollar to cover admin costs and profit; at 93% there is almost nothing left.

Medicaid (health cover for low-income Americans, run by states) is the core: 11.9m members. The Marketplace (Ambetter) sells subsidised individual plans under the Affordable Care Act. Medicare covers people over 65, mostly through stand-alone drug plans (Part D) at Centene.

Two technical mechanisms drive surprises. Risk adjustment moves money between insurers depending on how sick their members are, and the data arrives months after the year. State Medicaid rates are reset with a lag, so when costs jump the insurer absorbs them for a while.
macro_long: US health policy moved against Centene in 2025-2026. The enhanced ACA premium tax credits expired at the end of 2025, and Marketplace membership fell from 5.5m to 3.4m. Healthier members tend to leave first, which worsens the risk pool.

The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (July 2025) brings Medicaid work requirements and more frequent eligibility checks from end-2026. Fewer members means less revenue, and the members who remain are usually sicker.

Medical cost trends rose across the industry: behavioural health, home health and expensive drugs. On the positive side, the final 2027 Medicare Advantage rate notice (+2.48%) was much better than the January proposal.

The lag rule meant FY2024 accounts were used, before the 2025 collapse. EV/Sales is structurally low for any insurer (about $195bn of revenue on a $33bn market cap) and says nothing about margins. A revision or quality filter (estimate momentum, HBR trend, goodwill-to-equity) would have flagged the break.
note.bear_long: Even after the recovery, the bear case is credible: membership is shrinking, Medicaid margins are negative on an HBR basis, 2026 includes one-offs, and only $175m of cash sits outside regulated subsidiaries.
glossary: Health benefits ratio (HBR)
Medical costs divided by premium revenue; the core margin measure for an insurer.
Risk adjustment
Transfers between insurers based on members' health status, settled after the plan year.
Medicaid / Medicare
US public health programmes for low-income people (states) and for people over 65 (federal).
Guidance floor
A 'greater than' figure: the company commits to a minimum, not a midpoint.
interview: Your model held Centene through a 2025 collapse. What does that tell you?
That lagged trailing multiples cannot see a fast fundamental break. The fix is to add a quality or revision signal, not to drop value.
The stock doubled from its low. Wasn't the model right?
The outcome was good, but for reasons the model did not measure: repricing and policy. I judge the process, not the outcome.
Why Neutral now?
13x a 2026 floor that includes one-offs, shrinking membership and no 2027 guidance: upside and downside look balanced.
What one metric would you watch?
The Medicaid benefits ratio. Below about 92% the earnings recovery is real; stuck near 93.5% it is not.

name: Orient Overseas (International)
headline: The highest value score in our universe, on peak-cycle earnings: a call on freight rates, not a cheap compounder
one_liner: OOIL (OOCL) had the top score of our entire universe in December 2025. The screen saw a P/E under 4x on FY2024 profit; FY2025 profit then fell 41% and H1 2026 another 24%. A 2026 war shock lifted freight rates again, but on normalised earnings the stock is not cheap. We hold the model weight floor and expect mean reversion.
thesis: Why the model bought it

With a six-month lag, the December 2025 score used FY2024 accounts: EBIT of US$2.6bn. FY2025 then delivered US$1.5bn. On the earnings actually being produced the stock was about 40% less cheap than the screen showed.
Earnings are a freight rate times a volume
Profit rose more than 60-fold from the 2019 operating base to the 2022 peak, then fell 86% in a year. A screen that buys the lowest trailing P/E in shipping buys just after peak earnings.
2026 was rescued by a war, not by value
The US-Iran war and Hormuz disruption pushed Asia-US rates up 109% by June 2026 and Q3 liner revenue up 45%. Fleet growth (4.6%) still runs ahead of demand (4.1%), and ships are returning to Suez.
variant: Net cash of US$4.5bn makes it safe.
Yard and charter commitments (~US$7.5bn) exceed net cash; FCF after leases was negative in 2025 and H1 2026.
The dividend yield is attractive.
Dividends follow profits: US$10.56 per share in 2022, US$1.14 in 2025. A trailing yield overstates future income.
Q3 2026 shows a new up-cycle.
The spike is geopolitical. Port fees on Chinese operators may return on 10 November 2026.
business: A pure-play liner: 139 vessels and 1.15m TEU of capacity at end-2025, member of the Ocean Alliance.
Trans-Pacific (most US policy exposure), Asia-Europe, Trans-Atlantic and Intra-Asia (most volume).
COSCO Shipping holds 71.07% and Shanghai International Port Group 9.06%: the free float is about 20%.
No bank debt; US$5.8bn of cash against US$1.3bn of lease liabilities at June 2026.

note.intro: OOIL is the second case study in this set. It had the highest value score in our whole developed-market universe in December 2025 (z-score +5.5, ranked first of 199 Industrials) and shows why trailing multiples mislead in cyclical industries. This note explains how a container line makes money, why its profits swing so much, and how to normalise earnings before calling a cyclical stock cheap.
business_long: OOIL owns OOCL, a container shipping line. It moves standard containers (measured in TEU, twenty-foot equivalent units) on fixed routes between Asia, North America and Europe. Revenue is the number of containers carried (liftings) times the freight rate per container.

Costs are mostly fixed in the short run: ships, crews, port charges and fuel. So when freight rates double, almost all the extra revenue becomes profit, and when rates fall, profits collapse. That operating leverage is why profit went from about US$0.2bn (2019 operations) to US$10bn (2022) and back to US$1.5bn (2025).

COSCO Shipping, a Chinese state-owned group, controls 71% of OOIL. The group has no bank debt and a large cash pile, but it is spending heavily on new ships (contracted capex of US$5.45bn at June 2026), much of it at COSCO-linked yards.
macro_long: Freight rates depend on the balance between ship supply and trade demand, and on disruptions that lengthen routes. Since 2024 ships have avoided the Red Sea and sailed around the Cape of Good Hope, which absorbs capacity. In 2026 the US-Iran war disrupted the Strait of Hormuz and Asia-US spot rates more than doubled.

Underneath, the industry is oversupplied: the fleet grows 4.6% in 2026 against 4.1% demand growth, with large orderbooks still to deliver. When ships return to Suez, effective capacity jumps and rates fall.

US policy adds risk for a Chinese-controlled carrier. Section 301 port fees of US$50 per net ton took effect in October 2025, were suspended for a year in November 2025, and may resume on 10 November 2026.

glossary: TEU
Twenty-foot equivalent unit: the standard measure of container volume.
Liftings
Number of containers carried in the period.
Normalised earnings
Average earnings over a full cycle, used to value a cyclical company.
Operating leverage
High fixed costs mean small revenue changes produce large profit changes.
interview: Why is a stock with a P/E under 4x not cheap?
Because the 'E' is a peak. Normalised over the cycle, profit is about US$1.3bn and the stock trades near 10x.
What does this case teach about your model?
A value composite needs a cyclical adjustment, such as normalised or average earnings for deep cyclicals.
What would change your view?
A price below normalised value, an orderbook cut with cash returned, or real capacity discipline.
Why Underweight and not Sell?
Disruption can last and the cash could come back as a special dividend. The risk is asymmetric but not one-way.

headline: Japan's nuclear leader is modestly cheap, once record 2025 profits are normalised
one_liner: Kansai runs 45% of Japan's operating nuclear capacity and trades at 0.85x book. But FY2025 was a peak year (84% nuclear capacity factor, fuel time-lag gains), and the company's own plan guides ordinary profit down 44% in FY2026 and ROE to about 8-9%. On normalised returns the upside is single-digit: we keep the model weight.
thesis: A unique asset
Seven pressurised-water reactors (6,578 MW), 45% of Japan's operating nuclear capacity. Each point of capacity factor is worth about ¥5.7bn of ordinary profit.
But the trailing earnings are a peak
FY2025 ordinary profit of ¥518.5bn benefited from an 84% capacity factor and fuel time-lag gains. The FY2026 guide is ¥290bn and the 2026-28 plan averages ¥270bn. Trailing P/E overstates value.
Capital returns are steady, not large
A 25-35% payout, a progressive dividend (¥80 guided) and at least ¥270bn of returns over FY2026-28, funded partly by asset sales. Yield 2.9%.

At 0.85x book it must be cheap.

note.intro: Kansai Electric entered the portfolio in June 2025 and ranked first of 59 utilities in December 2025. Unlike the case studies, it is a solid business; the question is how much of its cheapness survives once you normalise a record year. This note explains how a Japanese utility earns money, why nuclear availability dominates the numbers, and why our call is Neutral.
business_long: Kansai Electric supplies the Osaka-Kyoto-Kobe region. It generates power (nuclear, thermal and hydro), sells it to households and businesses, and owns the regulated transmission and distribution network through Kansai T&D.

Its edge is nuclear: seven reactors at Takahama, Ohi and Mihama, 45% of Japan's operating nuclear capacity. Nuclear power is cheap once plants run, so every point of capacity factor (the share of the year the reactors produce) adds about ¥5.7bn of profit. When reactors are in outage, the company burns more expensive fuel.

Japanese utilities report 'ordinary profit', which includes financial income and equity-method results. Fuel costs are passed to customers with a 3-5 month lag, which creates 'time-lag' gains when fuel prices fall and losses when they rise.
macro_long: Japan restarted nuclear plants slowly after Fukushima (2011). Kansai is the most advanced, but older units (Takahama 1 and 2 are over 50 years old) need regulatory approvals and are exposed to court injunctions.

The 2026 Middle East conflict pushed crude to an average of $108 a barrel in H1 FY2026, against an $80 plan assumption, and the yen weakened to ¥160. Combined with outages, ordinary profit fell 65% in H1.
Data centres and electrification are the long-term demand story, but they have not yet moved total Kansai-area demand, which is flat at about 133 TWh.

Its P/E was 5.8x against 18.4x for its peers. Both risk-based portfolios gave it the 4% cap because utilities lower portfolio volatility.

glossary: Capacity factor
Actual output divided by the maximum possible output over a period.
Ordinary profit
Japanese profit line: operating profit plus financial income and equity-method results.
Fuel time lag
Delay between fuel-cost changes and the tariff adjustment passed to customers.
Justified P/B
(ROE − g) / (cost of equity − g): the price-to-book a company deserves for its returns.
interview: Why is Kansai Neutral when it screens as the cheapest utility?
The screen used peak FY2024-25 earnings. On normalised ROE of about 6.5% the justified P/B is about 0.92x, close to today's 0.85x.
What is the most important number for Kansai?
The nuclear capacity factor: each point is worth about ¥5.7bn of ordinary profit.
Why did the minimum-variance portfolio give it 4%?
Utilities have low volatility and low correlation with cyclicals, so a risk-minimising optimiser loads them to the cap.
What would make you upgrade?
Capacity factor back above 75% and ROE guidance above 9%, with no new equity raise.
